samples.summary: `GET /start` hands the login nonce to any unauthenticated local client, widening the nonce-theft surface the change claims to close
samples.evidence:
The new route answers the *first* request on the loopback port with `302 Location: ` (login.ts:277-279) with no authentication, no caller identification and no rate limit. Attack: a local process polls `curl -s -D- http://127.0.0.1:

/start` across the ephemeral port range (the port is trivially discoverable — it is printed to stderr at login.ts:67 and is the same port that appears in the browser's authorize URL) and wins the race against `open()`, which needs hundreds of ms to spawn a browser. It now holds the 32-byte nonce, so it can (a) drive its own `GET ${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=&cliState=` — the backend accepts any well-formed nonce (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:70) and echoes it on the loopback redirect (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:130-135) — and (b) deliver `GET http://127.0.0.1:

/callback?code=&state=` to the victim's listener, which passes `stateMatches` (login.ts:322) and settles the login, so the victim's `session.json` is written with the *attacker's* tokens/workspace (login.ts:168). The previous design leaked the nonce only through `open()`'s argv, which is world-readable only on Linux `/proc//cmdline`; an HTTP endpoint on loopback is readable by every process on every OS (macOS and Windows both hide other users' argv), so for macOS/Windows this is a new exposure rather than a mitigated one. `docs/design/rest-api.md:379` concedes the race but asserts it "breaks the login visibly" — the only visible artifact is a 410 page in the browser, after which the CLI still prints a successful `Logged in as `.

samples.summary: The `--allow-unbound-callback` downgrade lever the comment claims to remove is still attacker-reachable: an attacker-sent nonce-less callback rewrites the timeout message into the "re-run with --allow-unbound-callback" nudge
samples.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by *any* caller of `GET /callback?code=x` with no `state` (login.ts:306-315) — reachable by every local process and every page the browser visits — and it is the sole selector for the timeout error text (login.ts:378-380), which is `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` = "...re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` to accept an unbound callback" (login.ts:222-226). Attack: a local process (1) consumes `/start` so the genuine browser leg can never produce a callback (login.ts:272-275 → 410), (2) sends one nonce-less `/callback?code=…`, (3) waits 30 s. The user is told, in the CLI's own voice, that the server is too old and to re-run with the flag; on that re-run `options.allowUnbound` is true, so the very next nonce-less callback the attacker sends is accepted outright (login.ts:306 short-circuits, 328-370 settles) and the attacker's code becomes the victim's session. The in-code rationale ("letting one of those abort the login … would hand an attacker a downgrade lever", login.ts:298-305) and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 assert this lever is gone; it is only delayed by the 30-second timeout. Deciding the message from an attacker-settable flag is the defect — the skew signal should come from something the attacker cannot set (e.g. the absence of the echo on a callback whose nonce matched, or a server capability probe).

samples.summary: The loopback listener validates no `Host`/`Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` header, so a page the browser visits can consume the single-use nonce hand-off (login denial), and a DNS-rebound origin reaches a secret-serving endpoint
samples.evidence:
The request handler only inspects `req.url` (login.ts:262) and never looks at `req.headers`. Consequences: (1) any page the victim's browser visits can `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:

/start', {mode:'no-cors'})` or embed an iframe across the ephemeral port range; the request is a simple GET so no preflight applies, `startConsumed` flips (login.ts:277) and the real browser leg gets the 410 — a remote-page denial of every `wafflebase login`, plus a nudge into the retry loop that finding #2 weaponises. (2) Because no `Host` allow-list is enforced, the endpoint is reachable under an attacker-controlled hostname via DNS rebinding, i.e. from a same-origin JS context, which is precisely the configuration in which the same-origin argument in docs/design/cli.md:214-217 no longer holds; I could not construct a concrete browser primitive that reads a 302 `Location` even same-origin (`redirect:'manual'` yields an opaqueredirect), which is why confidence is low, but a loopback endpoint whose whole purpose is to serve a secret should not be answerable to requests whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:` or that carry a cross-site `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site`. Also unrestricted by method: a HEAD or POST to `/start` consumes it too.

samples.summary: stderr no longer shows where the browser is actually being sent, so a hijacked `--server` value is invisible to the user
samples.evidence: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${startUrl}`)` plus "visit the URL above" (login.ts:67-68) now prints only `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start`; the target host is hidden inside the `Location` header built at login.ts:66/209-212 from an unvalidated `server` string. Previously the printed line contained `${server}/auth/github?...`, which let a user notice they were about to authenticate against an attacker-supplied server (e.g. a pasted `wafflebase login --server https://evil.example` or a doctored profile). The redirect target is also unvalidated for scheme/host and interpolated straight into a response header, so a `server` value containing CR/LF makes `res.writeHead(302, { Location: authorizeUrl })` (login.ts:278) throw `ERR_INVALID_CHAR` inside the request handler — an uncaught exception rather than a clean error. Printing the resolved authorize *host* alongside the loopback URL restores the check without reintroducing the nonce.

samples.summary: The nonce-bearing 302 is served without `Cache-Control: no-store` / `Referrer-Policy`
samples.evidence: login.ts:278 writes the redirect with only `Location`. A 302 is not cacheable by default, so this is hardening rather than a live leak, but an endpoint whose response header is a one-time secret should say `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` so no intermediary, extension, or bfcache copy of the authorize URL outlives the 30-second login.
searchedFor: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:261-371 — the only writeHead calls in the listener
grep for Cache-Control / Referrer-Policy in packages/cli/src

verdict.reason: Verified as described. login.ts:266-281 answers the first unauthenticated request on the loopback port with a 302 to the nonce-carrying authorize URL (buildAuthorizeUrl at 204-213 embeds the 32-byte state minted at line 46); no caller identification, no rate limit, and the port is printed to stderr (line 67) and is scannable. That nonce is the only binding protecting the listener: /callback accepts any code whose state matches (322-326), settles the login (367-370), and the code is exchanged and written to session.json (86-90, 168). Backend legs confirm exploitability: github-auth.guard.ts:61-78 accepts any well-formed cliState for any caller-supplied port, and auth.controller.ts:130-135 echoes the nonce back on the 127.0.0.1 redirect. verdict.reason: The finding is accurate at every cited location. `sawUnboundCallback` is latched in the `received === null && !options.allowUnbound` branch (login.ts:306-316), which is reached before any nonce comparison and requires only a `code` param — so any local process or any page the browser visits can set it via `GET http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback?code=x`. That flag is the sole selector for the timeout error text (login.ts:373-385), and the text it selects, UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE (login.ts:222-226), instructs the user to "re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`". `/start` is single-use (login.ts:272-276, 410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE), so an attacker who follows it first guarantees the genuine browser leg never produces a callback and the 30 s timeout path is what the user sees. On the re-run, `options.allowUnbound` is true, so line 306 short-circuits, the mismatch check at 322 is skipped for a null state, and control falls to 328-370 where `callbackResolve(code)` accepts the attacker's authorization code as the victim's session. No guard exists elsewhere: `stateMatches` (188-196) is never reached for a nonce-less callback, and there is no origin check, rate limit, or requirement that a nonce-matched callback be seen first. The in-file rationale (login.ts:298-305) and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 both assert this nudge must not be attacker-triggerable, but the timeout branch reintroduces it. This is an auth-downgrade weakness in the security lane; major severity fits since it needs the user to follow the CLI's own instruction.

verdict.reason: Verified the absence directly: the handler at packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:261-371 reads only req.url (line 262) and never touches req.headers or req.method, so there is no Host allow-list, Origin check, or Sec-Fetch-Site check. The server comes from node:http createServer (login.ts:2) with no wrapper/middleware that could add the check indirectly; the only header reads in packages/cli are on outbound responses (src/client/http-client.ts:277) and in a test (test/login-callback.test.ts:25). The only Sec-Fetch/CSRF header logic in the repo is vendored hono code under .trusted/scripts/agent/node_modules, unreachable from the CLI. Consequence is concrete for the denial leg: any request to /start, from any origin and by any method, flips startConsumed (line 277), after which the genuine browser leg gets 410 (line 273) and the login fails — a remote page can do this with a no-cors GET across the ephemeral port range. The design doc at docs/design/cli.md:206-223 leans on the same-origin policy only for preventing a visited page from *reading* the 302 Location; it does not address consumption, and it implicitly assumes the endpoint is only addressed as 127.0.0.1:<port>, which a DNS-rebound hostname breaks since Node answers any Host. The secret-read-via-rebinding half is unproven (no browser primitive to read a 302 Location), matching the finding's own low confidence, but the missing Host/Origin allow-list on a nonce-serving loopback endpoint is a real security weakness in the crypto/auth lane. No counterexample found anywhere in the repo.

finding.summary: Attacker-triggerable "unbound callback" path aborts the login and advertises the flag that disables the nonce binding
finding.evidence: The no-`state` branch is reachable by anyone who can reach the loopback listener, which is exactly the threat model the nonce exists for: a malicious page in the browser (cross-origin ``/`fetch(..., {mode:'no-cors'})` to `http://127.0.0.1:/callback?code=ATTACKER_CODE`) or any local process can send a callback with no `state` at all. login.ts:263-271 then calls `callbackReject(new Error(UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE))`, killing the in-flight login, and UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE (login.ts:216-220) asserts a cause the CLI cannot actually distinguish ("The server ... did not echo this invocation's nonce") and offers the remedy "re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`". A user who follows the CLI's own advice re-runs with `allowUnbound: true`, at which point the identical nonce-less spray IS accepted (the `received === null` guard is skipped) and the attacker's authorization code is exchanged at `${server}/auth/cli/exchange` and written to `~/.wafflebase/session.json` as the user's session — the precise attack the nonce was added to prevent. Net: an attacker can (a) DoS every login attempt and (b) social-engineer the control off using the tool's own error text. A missing `state` should be treated like a wrong one (400, do not settle, keep waiting) with the version-skew hint deferred to the 30-second timeout, so an injected request cannot cause the abort or the downgrade advice.

verdict.reason: The finding's central presence claim is false. It asserts the nonce-less `/callback` branch calls `callbackReject(new Error(UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE))`, aborting the in-flight login and steering the user at `--allow-unbound-callback`. In this repository that branch (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:296-317) writes a 400, sets a `sawUnboundCallback` flag, emits a single warning that explicitly does NOT mention the flag, and returns without settling the callback promise — the real callback can still arrive and resolve. A grep for `callbackReject` across packages/cli/src yields only the declaration (245), assignment (253), and the 30-second timeout handler (376): there is no abort path reachable from an injected request. The version-skew message is substituted only at the timeout, when nothing else ever arrived (login.ts:373-385) — which is exactly the fix the finding prescribes. Therefore neither claimed impact exists: an injected nonce-less request cannot DoS a login attempt, and the flag advice is not surfaced to the user on an attacker-triggerable path (the 400 body containing it is returned only to the sender of that request). The `allowUnbound` acceptance at line 306 is a documented, explicit per-invocation opt-out that still rejects a present-but-wrong nonce (login.ts:322-326). The in-repo behavior contracts confirm this: packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:92-119 asserts 400 + one warning without the flag + no settlement + real callback still wins, and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 documents the same semantics.

finding.summary: The URL printed for headless copy-paste omits `cliState`, so the documented headless flow always produces an unbound callback and steers users to `--allow-unbound-callback`
finding.evidence: login.ts:71-76 builds `oauthUrl` with `&cliState=<nonce>` but prints `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` — deliberately nonce-stripped — and the old "If the browser does not open, visit the URL above." line was removed; the full URL is printed only in the `catch` around `open()`. `open()` frequently resolves successfully while opening nothing (SSH sessions with a stub xdg-open, WSL, containers), and docs/design/cli.md:176 still documents step 3 as "(also prints URL for copy-paste in headless environments)". A user who copies the printed URL starts a flow with no `cliState`, so `normalizeCliState` returns undefined (github-auth.guard.ts:70), `state.cliState` is falsy at auth.controller.ts:130, and the loopback redirect carries no `state`. The CLI then aborts with UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE, which blames the server and recommends `--allow-unbound-callback` — training the ordinary headless user to run every login with the anti-injection binding disabled. The printed line should carry the full URL (or omit the copy-paste affordance entirely and say so).

verdict.reason: The code described does not exist in this tree. login.ts:66-68 prints the loopback `startUrl` (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start`) AND still prints 'If the browser does not open, visit the URL above.' — the line the finding says was removed. The nonce-stripped `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` string appears only inside buildAuthorizeUrl (login.ts:210-212), always concatenated with `&cliState=`, and that URL is never printed anywhere; the catch around open() (login.ts:73-75) prints no URL at all. The printed `/start` URL 302-redirects to the full cliState-carrying authorize URL (login.ts:266-281, asserted in test/login-callback.test.ts:184-206), so a copied printed URL yields a nonce-BOUND flow, not an unbound one. The claimed steering to `--allow-unbound-callback` also cannot occur from this path: UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE is only raised at timeout when an actual state-less GET /callback set sawUnboundCallback (login.ts:306-317, 373-385); otherwise the failure message is 'Login timed out.' docs/design/cli.md:175-177 documents exactly the /start-then-302 behavior the code implements, not the quoted text.

mergedFrom.summary: The nonce reaches the browser through `open(url)`, exposing it via argv to other local users on Linux

finding.summary: The anti-injection nonce is not secret from the very attacker it targets — it is handed to the browser via argv and printed to stderr
finding.evidence: The whole defence added here rests on `state` (login.ts:40) being unguessable by "another local process" (comment login.ts:33-39, docs/design/cli.md, rest-api.md risk table). But the nonce is embedded in `oauthUrl` (login.ts:44-46), which is (a) printed with `console.error` (login.ts:47) and (b) passed to `open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:52), which spawns the browser/xdg-open with the full URL as a command-line argument. On Linux/macOS with default settings any local process — including one running as a different unprivileged user — can read that argv (`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `ps auxww`). Attack: local attacker polls `ps` during `wafflebase login`, reads `cliState=<nonce>` and `port=<port>`, then starts their own flow `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&cliState=<stolen nonce>` authenticating as the ATTACKER's GitHub account. The backend mints a code for the attacker's user and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=…&state=<stolen nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:130-135); `stateMatches` (login.ts:210) passes, the victim's CLI exchanges the attacker's code and saves the attacker's tokens as the session — the exact code-injection/session-fixation this change claims to close. A value-echo nonce cannot fix this because the value the CLI expects is the value it leaks; the standard fix is PKCE (CLI sends `code_challenge` in the URL, keeps the verifier in-process, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` requires the verifier so a code minted for another challenge cannot be redeemed).

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual premise is false in this repository. There is no `oauthUrl` variable; the nonce-bearing authorize URL (built at login.ts:210 via `buildAuthorizeUrl`, assigned at login.ts:66) is never printed and never passed to `open()`. Both `console.error` (login.ts:67) and `open(...)` (login.ts:72) receive `startUrl`, which is `http://127.0.0.1:${addr.port}/start` (login.ts:399) and contains no nonce. The nonce reaches the browser only through the in-process single-use 302 at login.ts:266-281 (`startConsumed` guard, login.ts:272-277), so an attacker reading `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` or `ps auxww` sees only the `/start` URL and cannot learn `cliState`. The described attack chain (steal nonce from argv/stderr, replay `GET /auth/github?...&cliState=<stolen>`, pass `stateMatches` at login.ts:188-196) therefore cannot be initiated. Test packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:190-191 asserts `startUrl` does not contain the nonce. The only related residual risk — a local process racing the browser to `GET /start` — is a different, loud-failure attack already documented at login.ts:52-65 and docs/design/rest-api.md:378, and is not what this finding claims. Grep across all .ts/.js files shows exactly one construction of the nonce-bearing URL and no other `open()`/print path.
